content: Preterm infants are at a higher risk of depleting their body iron stores much earlier than healthy term newborns. To prevent iron deficiency anemia, it is a common practice to provide enteral iron supplementation to preterm and low birth weight infants. However, it remains uncertain whether iron supplementation in these infants leads to improvements in growth and neurodevelopmental outcomes. There is concern that excessive exogenous iron may contribute to oxidative injury in preterm infants, potentially causing or worsening conditions such as necrotizing enterocolitis and retinopathy of prematurity. Additionally, the optimal dose, timing of initiation, and duration of iron supplementation are not well established. The primary objective of this review was to assess the impact of prophylactic enteral iron supplementation on growth and neurodevelopmental outcomes in preterm and low birth weight infants. Secondary objectives included evaluating whether iron supplementation improves hematological parameters and reduces other causes of morbidity and mortality. The review employed the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and CINAHL were searched, along with conference proceedings and previous reviews. The search covered studies up to August 2011. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials comparing enteral iron supplementation with no supplementation, or different regimens of supplementation, in preterm or low birth weight infants were included. Data were extracted using standard Cochrane methods, and trial quality was independently assessed by two reviewers. Data synthesis involved calculating risk ratios (RRs), risk differences (RDs), and weighted mean differences (WMDs). When methodological or result-related data were incomplete, study authors were contacted for additional information. A total of 26 studies involving 2726 infants were included in the analysis. The heterogeneity of participants, methods, and results limited the ability to perform extensive quantitative synthesis. Among the 21 studies comparing iron supplementation with controls, none evaluated neurodevelopmental outcomes. Of the 13 studies reporting at least one growth parameter, only one low-quality study demonstrated a significant benefit of iron supplementation. Regarding hematological outcomes, no benefit of iron supplementation was observed within the first 8.5 weeks of postnatal life in 16 trials, except for two low-quality studies. Beyond this age, most studies reported higher mean hemoglobin levels in iron-supplemented infants. A limited quantitative meta-analysis suggested that hemoglobin concentration in iron-supplemented infants was approximately 6 g/L higher at six to nine months of age. One study comparing high-dose and low-dose iron supplementation monitored neurodevelopmental outcomes for one year but found no significant differences between the groups. Another study comparing early versus late initiation of iron supplementation found no differences in cognitive outcomes but reported a higher rate of abnormal neurological examinations in the late supplementation group at five years of age. Studies comparing high and low doses of iron indicated no clear hematological advantage in exceeding standard doses of 2-3 mg/kg/day. The available evidence suggests that iron supplementation in preterm and low birth weight infants results in slightly higher hemoglobin levels, improved iron stores, and a reduced risk of iron deficiency anemia compared to unsupplemented infants. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether iron supplementation provides long-term benefits for neurodevelopmental outcomes and growth. The optimal timing and duration of iron supplementation remain uncertain.
